"Alka, look at this! A remote job. Just like videos and rate restaurants. Eight hundred a task!"
"Who sent it?"
"A woman called Neha on a chat app. She said I was selected."
"Selected from what? Did you apply?"
Aditi paused. "No. But the first two tasks paid. Look, the money came."
"And now?"
"Now I have to deposit five thousand to unlock the 'premium tasks'. Then I earn triple."
Alka put down her tea. "Aditi, why would a stranger pay you eight hundred to like a video?"
"...To hook me?"
"Exactly. They pay small, then ask for big. Real jobs don't make you pay to earn. What's the company's name?"
Aditi searched it. No registration. No website. Just the chat group. Her stomach sank. She had so wanted it to be real.
"Too good to be true," she said quietly, and blocked Neha's number.

qa.a: Five thousand.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she searched the company and found nothing?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and uneasy, her stomach sinking, because she had so wanted the job to be real.

qa.q: What questions helped Aditi see the trap?
qa.a: Why a stranger would pay her to like videos, whether she had applied, and whether the company was registered, plus the fact that real jobs don't make you pay to earn.

passage:
I'm Bhupen, and last winter a man I'd met in an online chess group started telling me about his "crypto arbitrage". He was friendly, sent me screenshots, said my money would double in sixty days. I'd had a bad year. The idea of doubling felt like a door opening.
I told my friend Sangeeta about it over chai. She didn't laugh. She just asked, "Why would he share a secret that makes money for free?" I didn't have an answer.
That night I looked up the platform he recommended. It wasn't registered with any regulator I could find. Its website was two months old. The "reviews" all used the same sentences.
Looking back, what hooked me wasn't greed exactly. It was hope. I wanted something to go right. That's what the scam was built on. I stopped replying to him, reported his profile to the group admins, and told Sangeeta she'd probably saved me a lot.

qa.q: How long was the platform's website, according to Bhupen?
qa.a: Two months old.

qa.q: What made Bhupen want to believe the offer?
qa.a: Bhupen felt hopeful after a bad year, and the idea of doubling money felt like a door opening.

qa.q: How did Bhupen check the offer?
qa.a: Bhupen asked why a stranger would share free money, looked for the platform's registration, and noticed the website was new and the reviews repeated.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see her own question afterwards?
qa.a: Sangeeta may feel relieved and glad that one simple question helped Bhupen step back.

grounding: An offer of double returns works on hope; the protagonist asks why a stranger would give money away, checks registration and treats it as a trap.

Legal-aid volunteer's note, Wednesday.
Zainab came to the clinic with a thick folder. Three weeks ago, fifty thousand was taken from her account through a fake app. She reported it to her bank the same day. Since then, the helpline has told her "under process" four times. The last agent, Thomas, said, "Ma'am, there's nothing more I can do," and ended the call.
She was tired but not giving up. She had kept every complaint number, the dates of each call and screenshots.
We wrote a formal complaint letter to the bank's grievance officer with the timeline attached, and I explained that if there was no satisfactory reply in the time the bank's rules allow, she could escalate to the banking ombudsman. She also filed on the cybercrime portal, which she had not yet done.
She left calmer, with a checklist of follow-up dates. We'll review her reply together.

qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when she came to the clinic?
qa.a: She was tired and frustrated by the cold responses, but still determined not to give up.

Indu's diary, day 19.
Another call to the payment platform's support line. 42 minutes on hold. The agent read out the same script: "Your case is being reviewed." I asked for the case officer's name. "Not available." I wanted to scream.
Jeevan came over with dinner and found me with my head on the table. "Just forget it, it's gone," he said. I nearly agreed.
But then I opened my notes. Nineteen days of dates, reference numbers, names.
Things I did tonight:
- wrote a formal email to the platform's grievance officer, with all the reference numbers attached
- printed the timeline so I don't have to remember it in my head
- set a reminder: if no proper answer by the date in their policy, escalate to the ombudsman
- filed the cybercrime report number in the same folder
Still angry. But organised angry. Jeevan is helping me make a tracking sheet. Not despairing.

In Anjali's small town near Sagar, everyone knew everyone. So when the loan app's recovery agents started calling nine times a day, threatening to message her "whole contact list", her hands shook every time the phone buzzed. She'd borrowed a small amount for her mother's medicines. The interest had become monstrous.
Another app offered her a quick loan to pay the first. She almost pressed accept.
Her brother Karthik found her staring at it. "Don't. That's how people drown."
They sat together on the verandah. Karthik helped her record every call and screenshot every threat. He said the threats were harassment, not a normal part of lending, and it wasn't her fault.
The next day they went to the bank branch in town where Anjali had her salary account, and asked about a small personal loan with a proper schedule to close the app loan. The officer explained the options slowly. Anjali also filed a complaint about the harassment at the police station, with her screenshots.

qa.q: How many times a day did the recovery agents call?
qa.a: Nine times a day.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when the phone buzzed?
qa.a: She felt anxious and frightened, her hands shaking, afraid the agents would message her whole contact list.

qa.q: What did Anjali and Karthik do instead of taking another app loan?
qa.a: They recorded the calls and threats, asked her bank about a proper loan to close the app loan, and filed a harassment complaint at the police station.

qa.a: Karthik sees it as a trap that would deepen the debt, and feels protective of his sister.

Daniel sat down. "That'll make it worse, not stop."

The next morning, with Daniel beside him, he screenshotted every threatening message, saved the call logs, and went to his bank to ask whether they could offer a proper repayment plan. He also reported the app's harassment to the consumer protection agency. The threats didn't stop at once. But Emeka was no longer fighting them alone at 2 a.m.

Counsellor's note, workplace wellbeing clinic, Monday.
Charu came in saying she "couldn't breathe properly at night". It emerged that she has three EMIs and two credit card bills she has been hiding from her family for eight months. She had never added them up. She said she avoided opening the bank app.
I asked her to write every debt on paper, with the amount and interest rate. It took twenty minutes. She cried when she saw the total, then said, "At least now I know."
I referred her to the free credit counselling service our company offers, where a qualified counsellor can help her decide which debt to deal with first.
She asked whether she had to tell her parents. I asked if there was one person she trusted. She named her sister, Nikita. She called Nikita from the clinic before leaving.
Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.a: For eight months.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling before and after adding up the debts?

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor help Charu take?

Her heart raced. She almost paid everything in her account right then, just to make it stop.
Her flatmate Diego saw her face. "That's harassment. They can't threaten you like that. Don't pay in a panic."

Jana wrote to the lender's official complaints address, attaching the evidence and saying she wanted to agree a repayment plan in writing. She also reported the threats to the police.
Then she called her mother herself. "If anyone calls you about a loan, just hang up. I'm handling it." Her mother said, "Okay. Are you all right?" Jana finally cried.

At the district hospital in Belgaum, Kishore had been avoiding the canteen for a week. Vijay, a fellow lab technician, usually sat at the corner table. Three months ago, when Kishore's mother was admitted, Vijay had lent him twenty thousand without a second thought. Kishore had promised to repay in two months.
He hadn't. His salary was delayed, and he felt so ashamed that he'd started taking the back stairs.
On Friday, he forced himself to walk into the canteen and sit across from Vijay.
"Vijay, I owe you an apology. I haven't repaid, and I've been avoiding you. That's worse."
Vijay put down his cup. "I noticed. I thought I'd done something wrong."
"No. You saved my mother's treatment. Here's ten thousand today. The rest on the fifth of next month, when salary comes. I'll message you if anything changes."
Vijay nodded slowly. "Thanks for telling me. Next time, just tell me sooner."

Aparna posted another photo from a café today. Meanwhile, the fifteen thousand I lent her in March for "one month" is still gone, and she's ignored three messages. I feel so used. I keep writing angry texts and deleting them.

"Aparna, I lent you fifteen thousand in March. I need it back. Could you pay five thousand a month for three months, starting next week? If you can't, please just tell me honestly."

I'm Francis, and a year ago I was the guy with the latest everything. New phone on easy EMIs. Sneakers on buy-now-pay-later. A gaming chair I barely used. Each one felt small. "Only" nine hundred a month. "Only" twelve hundred.
Then one month my salary came and, after the auto-payments, I had almost nothing left for rent. I sat on the floor of my flat in Kochi and felt sick.
My friend Zubin came over and asked a simple question: "Which of these did you need?" I was honest. Maybe two.
Looking back, what helped was so boring. I wrote every EMI on one sheet and stuck it on my fridge. I made a rule for myself: anything non-essential waits a week in the cart. Most things I stopped wanting by day three.
It took eight months to clear the small EMIs. I still like nice things. But now I choose them.

qa.q: Where did Francis stick the sheet of EMIs?
qa.a: On the fridge.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling on the floor of the flat?
qa.a: Francis felt sick and alarmed, realising the small payments left almost nothing for rent.

qa.q: What habits helped Francis get out of lifestyle debt?
qa.a: Writing every EMI on one sheet, asking whether each item was a need, and waiting a week before buying anything non-essential.

passage: Yogesh, sit. You're upset that your wife hid that loan from you. I understand. Let me tell you about me and your aunt. When I was twenty-five, a young man just married, I found out that your Kamala-mami had borrowed from a moneylender to help her sister. She hadn't told me for six months. I felt like a fool in my own house. I shouted. She cried. I slept on the veranda. The next morning, I realised I didn't know why she'd done it. So I asked, and I listened. She had been afraid I'd say no. We sat with a notebook and wrote down every rupee owed. We went to the moneylender together and agreed on a schedule. And we made a promise: no secrets about money, even the embarrassing ones. We kept it for forty years. The secret hurt more than the debt, Yogesh. Ask for the full story. That's Pradeep-mama's advice.

qa.q: How long had Kamala-mami hidden the loan?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he found out about the loan?
qa.a: He felt betrayed and foolish, shouting and sleeping on the veranda.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Pradeep and Kamala-mami rebuild trust?
qa.a: Asking why she did it and listening, then writing every debt down, agreeing a schedule together, and making a no-secrets promise.

qa.q: How might Kamala-mami have felt while hiding the loan?
qa.a: She was probably afraid and anxious that Pradeep would refuse, which is why she kept it secret.

grounding: An elder recalls a partner's hidden debt, the hurt of secrecy, and rebuilding trust by listening, getting the full picture and agreeing honesty rules.
